newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: FORECAST-PLDT's first-half net seen slightly higher.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-PLDT's first-half net seen slightly higher.

text.p: Philippine Long Distance Telephone Co (PLDT) could post slightly higher profits for the first half of the year despite redundancy expenses and delays in introducing a new tariff structure, analysts said on Tuesday.

A Reuters poll of eight brokerage houses, four of whom predicted first half results, showed PLDT's net income from January to June was expected, on average, to rise 9.28 percent to 3.18 billion pesos.
For the first half of 1996, the Philippines biggest telephone company posted net income of 2.91 billion pesos. Full year net was 6.44 billion pesos.

"There will be a redundancy charge although we do not know how much (of this) PLDT will book for the first half. But operation-wise, there will be a 20 percent growth in recurring earnings for the first half," said Louie Hilado, analyst at ING Baring Securities.
PLDT's profits dropped 1.8 percent to 1.28 billion pesos in the first quarter of the year as the company paid 251.8 million pesos in a separation package to 3,000 employees.
Hilado said PLDT's revenue in the first half of the year from domestic calls was expected to grow by 30 percent although international revenue growth rate could be flat.
"Local revenue growth is fast catching up with international revenues and PLDT is on schedule in terms of installation of lines," said Alexis Cabel, analyst at Angping Securities.

Orion Squire-Capital Inc research head Cilette Liboro said international revenue would still account for the bulk at 52 percent, local calls revenue 31 percent and national long distance revenue 17 percent.

"People should look at operating income to see that for the year, there will actually be growth for PLDT. For 1997, we expect operating revenues at 32.37 billion pesos from last year's 28.66 billion," Liboro said.
Analysts said a number of issues had yet to be resolved to be able to determine with more certainty PLDT's financial performance for the year.

The accounting rates have yet to be settled. The United States Federal Communications Commission (FCC) has been pushing for a drastic reduction in the cost of international calls over the next two years. PLDT has been pushing for a more gradual reduction.
PLDT and its U.S. counterparts have yet to finalise a rate. Analysts had assumed a 15-20 percent cut for the year.

Secondly, PLDT has yet to secure the approval of the National Telecommunications Commission (NTC) for a rate restructuring that will help the carrier meet increasing competition and compensate for the lower accounting rates from international calls.
Most analysts said PLDT's income could pick up in the second half once its rate restructuring petition was accepted.
PLDT wants to raise basic phone charges and introduce a metering system for local calls. The NTC could try and temper the rise in local charges, analysts said.
"We expect a watered down version and it may take a while for PLDT to implement a metering scheme," said Saturnino Mejia, research head at Guoco Securities.
Despite uncertainties over rates and growing competition, PLDT was expected to hold on to its market share.
"It would take a while before competitors close in on PLDT and the pie is also getting bigger," said Mejia.
